etymology: From Old French ligue, from Latin ligare, to bind. Webster 1828: an alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defence. In the Authorized Version it names a binding political covenant — one that Israel was forbidden to make with the Canaanites and did make anyway, once, by deception.
biblical_def: A league in Scripture is a sworn alliance, and the Old Testament treats it as a matter of covenant loyalty rather than diplomacy. The command was flat: ye shall make no league with the inhabitants of this land; ye shall throw down their altars: but ye have not obeyed my voice (Judges 2:2). The Gibeonites therefore came disguised: We be come from a far country: now therefore make ye a league with us (Joshua 9:6). Israel’s error is recorded in the next verses — they asked the right question, Peradventure ye dwell among us; and how shall we make a league with you? (Joshua 9:7), and then failed to ask the LORD. Joshua made peace with them, and made a league with them, to let them live: and the princes of the congregation sware unto them (Joshua 9:15). The oath, once sworn, bound Israel for centuries, and God later avenged its breach by Saul. Not every league is forbidden: David made a league with them in Hebron before the LORD (2 Samuel 5:3), and Hiram and Solomon made a league together (1 Kings 5:12). The distinction is not between alliance and isolation but between an alliance that serves the covenant and one that binds God’s people to those whose altars they were commanded to throw down.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LEAGUE as an alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defence; and a combination or union of two or more parties for the maintenance of friendship or the prosecution of a common design.
webster_full: LEAGUE, n. [Fr. ligue; L. ligo, to bind.] — An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defence.
A combination or union of two or more parties for the maintenance of friendship and mutual interest, or for the prosecution of some design.
LEAGUE, v.i. — To unite or confederate, as princes or states.
The Latin root is to bind, and that is the biblical weight. Joshua 9 turns on the fact that a sworn league binds even when it was entered by mistake, because the oath was sworn before the LORD.
scriptures: Joshua 9:6
And they went to Joshua unto the camp at Gilgal, and said unto him, and to the men of Israel, We be come from a far country: now therefore make ye a league with us.
Joshua 9:15
And Joshua made peace with them, and made a league with them, to let them live: and the princes of the congregation sware unto them.
Judges 2:2
And ye shall make no league with the inhabitants of this land; ye shall throw down their altars: but ye have not obeyed my voice: why have ye done this?
2 Samuel 5:3
So all the elders of Israel came to the king to Hebron; and king David made a league with them in Hebron before the LORD: and they anointed David king over Israel.
1 Kings 5:12
And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him: and there was peace between Hiram and Solomon; and they two made a league together.
corruption_summary: The league is corrupted when the church enters binding alliances with those whose doctrine it is bound to oppose — the ecclesiastical version of Joshua 9 — and equally when a lawful alliance is treated as compromise and the church withdraws from every common cause.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 9 records the mechanism exactly. The Gibeonites do not argue Israel out of the command; they present a false account of who they are, with mouldy bread and cracked bottles, and Israel asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD (Joshua 9:14). The church makes the same mistake when it enters formal partnership with bodies whose confession it has not examined, on the strength of a shared cause and a friendly presentation. Ecumenical agreements that treat the Reformation’s doctrinal issues as settled or secondary are Gibeonite leagues: the terms are sworn before the question is asked. Paul’s rule for the church is not diplomatic but plain — come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord (2 Corinthians 6:17).

The opposite error must also be named, since Scripture records leagues God did not condemn. David’s covenant with the elders at Hebron was made before the LORD, and Solomon’s treaty with Hiram supplied the timber for the temple. Christians may join with unbelievers in civil work, trade, and the ordinary business of a shared society without sinning; the second commandment does not forbid a contract. The line falls where the alliance requires the church to leave altars standing that God commanded thrown down — that is, where the price of the league is the silencing of the church’s testimony.
roots_summary: The Hebrew word is berith, the ordinary word for covenant; the KJV renders it league where the parties are political and covenant where God is a party. The distinction is the translators’ and it is a useful one.
roots_lines: Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant, treaty, alliance; rendered league in Joshua 9:6, Judges 2:2, 2 Samuel 5:3, and 1 Kings 5:12.
The KJV’s choice of league for human-to-human treaties and covenant where God is a party is a translators’ convention, not a distinction in the Hebrew.
Hebrew karath berith — literally to cut a covenant, from the divided animals of Genesis 15; the same idiom underlies every league in these texts.
Hebrew shaba' (H7650) — to swear; the princes of the congregation sware unto them (Joshua 9:15) is what made the Gibeonite league unbreakable.
2 Samuel 21 records God’s judgment on Israel for Saul’s breach of that oath four centuries later — the measure of how binding a sworn league is.
usage: Ye shall make no league with the inhabitants of this land (Judges 2:2) — the command, with the charge of disobedience attached in the same verse.
Made a league with them, to let them live (Joshua 9:15) — sworn without asking counsel of the LORD, and binding thereafter.
King David made a league with them in Hebron before the LORD (2 Samuel 5:3) — a lawful covenant, made in God’s presence.

etymology: From Old Norse felagi, one who lays down money with another, a partner. Webster 1828: a companion; an associate; one of the same kind; and, in contempt, a mean or worthless man. The Authorized Version uses every one of those senses, including the contemptuous one — and once, astonishingly, of the Messiah beside the LORD of hosts.
biblical_def: Fellow in the KJV usually means the other man. Moses asks the aggressor, Wherefore smitest thou thy fellow? (Exodus 2:13). In Gideon’s camp one Midianite tells a dream and his fellow answered (Judges 7:14). In Saul’s rout every man's sword was against his fellow (1 Samuel 14:20). Jonah’s sailors speak every one to his fellow (Jonah 1:7). Ecclesiastes turns it into the argument for companionship: if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up (Ecclesiastes 4:10). The contemptuous sense is also biblical — Achish sneers, shall this fellow come into my house? (1 Samuel 21:15), and Jehu is called this mad fellow (2 Kings 9:11). But the weightiest use is Zechariah’s: Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man that is my fellow, saith the LORD of hosts: smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered (Zechariah 13:7). The Hebrew word there means one joined as an equal, and the LORD of hosts uses it of the shepherd He will smite — a verse our Lord quoted of Himself on the night He was betrayed.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives FELLOW as a companion; an associate; one of the same kind; an equal; and, in a lower sense, a mean or worthless man used in contempt. The KJV employs the full range.
webster_full: FELLOW, n. — A companion; an associate.
One of the same kind; as, the horse and his fellow.
An equal; one of the same rank or station.
A person of low condition; used in contempt; as, a mean fellow.

Webster’s third sense — an equal — is the one that makes Zechariah 13:7 so heavy. The LORD of hosts names the smitten shepherd as the man who is His fellow, which is a claim of equality no mere prophet could bear.
scriptures: Exodus 2:13
And when he went out the second day, behold, two men of the Hebrews strove together: and he said to him that did the wrong, Wherefore smitest thou thy fellow?
1 Samuel 14:20
And Saul and all the people that were with him assembled themselves, and they came to the battle: and, behold, every man's sword was against his fellow, and there was a very great discomfiture.
Ecclesiastes 4:10
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
Zechariah 13:7

Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man that is my fellow, saith the LORD of hosts: smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered: and I will turn mine hand upon the little ones.
Hebrews 1:9
Thou hast loved righteousness, and hated iniquity; therefore God, even thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss is a forgotten proof-text: Zechariah 13:7 is one of the strongest Old Testament witnesses to the deity of the Messiah, and it is now rarely preached as such.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The English word has drifted toward informality, but nothing is being contested. What has been lost is the doctrinal force of Zechariah 13:7. The LORD of hosts calls the shepherd the man that is my fellow — the Hebrew noun denotes an associate of the same standing, and it is used elsewhere in Leviticus of a man’s neighbour and equal. God does not call prophets or kings His fellow. That He does so of the smitten shepherd, and that our Lord applied the verse to Himself the night He was taken (Matthew 26:31), makes it a witness both to His deity and to the deliberateness of the cross: the sword is commanded to awake, and the commanding voice is the Father’s.

The principle to recover alongside it is Ecclesiastes 4:10, which the age needs and resists. Woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up is a plain argument against the isolated Christian life. The New Testament turns it into church membership — not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, bearing one another’s burdens, confessing faults one to another. A believer who has arranged his life so that no fellow is close enough to lift him has arranged it against the wisdom of this verse, and Hebrews 1:9 shows the pattern is not beneath the dignity of the Son, who is anointed above His fellows but is not without them.
roots_summary: Several words lie behind the English. Rea' is a neighbour or companion; 'amith in Zechariah 13:7 is an associate of equal standing; the Greek metochos in Hebrews 1:9 means a partner or partaker.
roots_lines: Hebrew rea' (H7453) — friend, neighbour, companion; wherefore smitest thou thy fellow? (Exodus 2:13), and the word in love thy neighbour.
Hebrew 'amith (H5997) — an associate, one of equal standing; the man that is my fellow (Zechariah 13:7), used elsewhere only in Leviticus.
Hebrew chaber (H2270) — a companion, one joined; behind the one will lift up his fellow (Ecclesiastes 4:10).
Greek metochos (G3353) — a partner, partaker; above thy fellows (Hebrews 1:9), and the word for those made partakers of Christ (Hebrews 3:14).
Greek hetairos (G2083) — comrade; our Lord’s address to Judas in Gethsemane, Friend, wherefore art thou come?
usage: Every man's sword was against his fellow (1 Samuel 14:20) — the confusion God sends on an enemy army.
Woe to him that is alone when he falleth (Ecclesiastes 4:10) — the case against the isolated life.
The man that is my fellow, saith the LORD of hosts (Zechariah 13:7) — an associate of equal standing with God, quoted by Christ of Himself.

etymology: Old English cyssan. Webster 1828: to salute with the lips; a salutation given with the lips, in token of affection or reverence. In Scripture the kiss is a public sign — of family affection, of covenant loyalty, of submission to a king, and, once, of the most famous treachery in history.
biblical_def: A kiss in Scripture is a formal sign given in public, not a private sentiment. Isaac calls Jacob near: Come near now, and kiss me, my son (Genesis 27:26), and it is the kiss that accompanies the blessing. Laban complains that Jacob fled and did not let him kiss my sons and my daughters (Genesis 31:28). Solomon makes it the reward of honest speech: Every man shall kiss his lips that giveth a right answer (Proverbs 24:26). Above all it is the sign of submission to a king, which is why the second psalm ends the way it does: Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him (Psalm 2:12). The nations that were raging are commanded to do homage. The New Testament makes the kiss the ordinary greeting of the congregation: Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you (Romans 16:16). And it records the counterfeit. Joab took Amasa by the beard with the right hand to kiss him and killed him (2 Samuel 20:9). Judas agreed a sign in advance (Matthew 26:48), and our Lord named it as he gave it: Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss? (Luke 22:48).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines KISS as a salute given with the lips, in token of affection, respect or reverence; and notes the ancient custom of kissing as an act of homage and of religious veneration.
webster_full: KISS, n. — A salute given with the lips; a common token of affection.
KISS, v.t. — To salute with the lips. To treat with fondness; to caress.
In ancient usage the kiss was also an act of homage or subjection rendered to a superior, and an act of religious veneration paid to idols — as in 1 Kings 19:18, of those who have not kissed Baal.
Webster’s note on homage is the key to Psalm 2:12. The command to kiss the Son is not an invitation to feel warmly toward Him; it is the demand that rebel kings submit.
scriptures: Genesis 27:26
And his father Isaac said unto him, Come near now, and kiss me, my son.
Psalm 2:12
Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him.
Proverbs 24:26
Every man shall kiss his lips that giveth a right answer.
Luke 22:48
But Jesus said unto him, Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?
Romans 16:16
Salute one another with an holy kiss. The churches of Christ salute you.
corruption_summary: Psalm 2:12 is corrupted when the kiss is read as devotional warmth rather than as the homage of a subject — which turns a command to rebel rulers into a private feeling, and empties the psalm of its politics.
corruption_paragraphs: The second psalm is addressed to kings and judges of the earth who are taking counsel against the LORD and against His anointed, and its conclusion is an ultimatum: Be wise now therefore, O ye kings… Kiss the Son, lest he be angry. The kiss commanded is the ancient gesture of a vassal to his sovereign. Read as an invitation to affectionate feeling, the psalm loses its argument, and with it the doctrine of the mediatorial kingship of Christ over the nations — that the risen Lord holds actual authority over states and rulers now, and not merely over private hearts. That doctrine is the ground of the Christian’s duty to the magistrate and of the magistrate’s duty to Christ, and it is why the Reformers preached this psalm to princes.

The counterfeit kiss is the second warning and it is aimed at the church. Joab’s greeting and Judas’s sign both used the outward form of covenant affection to accomplish betrayal, and our Lord’s question — betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss? — names the perversion exactly. Paul’s holy kiss is the redeemed form: a public greeting among people who genuinely belong to one another. The adjective is doing the work. A congregation with warm greetings and cold conduct has the form Judas used, and the letters that command the holy kiss also command that love be without dissimulation (Romans 12:9).
roots_summary: The Hebrew nashaq means to kiss and also to arm or equip, a homonym the Old Testament exploits; the Greek philema is the noun, and kataphileo, to kiss fervently, is what Judas did.
roots_lines: Hebrew nashaq (H5401) — to kiss; also, in a related form, to be armed or equipped, which is why some render Psalm 2:12 with the idea of doing homage.
Hebrew nashaq in 1 Kings 19:18 — the seven thousand which have not bowed unto Baal, and every mouth which hath not kissed him; the kiss as idolatrous homage.
Greek philema (G5370) — a kiss; the holy kiss of Romans 16:16, 1 Corinthians 16:20, and 1 Thessalonians 5:26.
Greek kataphileo (G2705) — to kiss fervently or repeatedly; used of Judas in Matthew 26:49 and of the woman at our Lord’s feet in Luke 7:38.

The Aramaic-influenced text of Psalm 2:12 has generated debate over Kiss the Son; the KJV’s rendering follows the reading the church has read messianically from the beginning, and Acts 4:25-26 quotes the psalm of Christ.
usage: Kiss the Son, lest he be angry (Psalm 2:12) — homage demanded of rulers, not affection invited from individuals.
Betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss? (Luke 22:48) — the sign of covenant loyalty used as the sign of betrayal.
Salute one another with an holy kiss (Romans 16:16) — the ordinary greeting of a congregation, and the adjective is not decorative.

etymology: From Latin separatio, a setting apart. Webster 1828: the act of separating; disjunction; the state of being separate. In the Authorized Version the noun is technical in three places — the Nazarite’s vow, the woman’s ceremonial uncleanness, and the water of separation made with the ashes of the red heifer.
biblical_def: Separation in the law is a defined period or a defined substance, not a mood. The Nazarite’s vow is measured in days of separation: All the days of his separation shall he eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk (Numbers 6:4), and the reason is stated without qualification: All the days of his separation he is holy unto the LORD (Numbers 6:8). When the term is complete he shall be brought unto the door of the tabernacle (Numbers 6:13). The second use is the woman’s ceremonial uncleanness, regulated in Leviticus 12 and 15 — every thing that she lieth upon in her separation shall be unclean (Leviticus 15:20). The third is a liquid: the water of separation, made from the ashes of the red heifer, which purified the man defiled by a dead body, and which paradoxically defiled the man who prepared it (Numbers 19:21). Ezekiel’s temple has the principle built into stone: a wall to make a separation between the sanctuary and the profane place (Ezekiel 42:20). The doctrine running through all four is that holiness has boundaries, and God draws them Himself.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SEPARATION as the act of separating or disjoining; the state of being separate; and, in law, a partial divorce. The KJV uses the noun in its ceremonial senses: a period of vow, a period of uncleanness, and a purifying water.
webster_full: SEPARATION, n. — The act of separating, or state of being separate; disjunction.
The operation of disuniting or decomposing substances; analysis.
In a legal sense, the parting of husband and wife without a dissolution of the marriage bond.

The biblical noun is narrower than Webster’s English. In Numbers 6 it names the whole period of the vow, so that the days themselves are called his separation — the man is not merely doing something separate; he is a separated thing for a term.
scriptures: Numbers 6:4
All the days of his separation shall he eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk.
Numbers 6:8
All the days of his separation he is holy unto the LORD.
Numbers 6:13
And this is the law of the Nazarite, when the days of his separation are fulfilled: he shall be brought unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation:
Numbers 19:21
And it shall be a perpetual statute unto them, that he that sprinkleth the water of separation shall wash his clothes; and he that toucheth the water of separation shall be unclean until even.
Ezekiel 42:20
He measured it by the four sides: it had a wall round about, five hundred reeds long, and five hundred broad, to make a separation between the sanctuary and the profane place.
corruption_summary: Separation is corrupted in two directions: by a church that has erased every boundary between the sanctuary and the profane, and by a separatism that keeps drawing new lines until it has divided from everyone but itself.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 42:20 states the purpose of a wall: to make a separation between the sanctuary and the profane place. The distinction is God’s, and a church that has lost it will not be more accessible but merely indistinguishable. The New Testament does not abolish the distinction; it relocates it, since the church is now the temple of the living God, which is why Paul quotes Isaiah at the Corinthians — come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you (2 Corinthians 6:17). What that requires is not withdrawal from society, which Paul explicitly denies in 1 Corinthians 5:10, but the refusal of unequal yokes and of tolerated sin within the assembly.

The opposite error has a long and unhappy history among those who take the doctrine seriously. Secondary separation — refusing fellowship not only with the unfaithful but with the faithful who have not refused them — has fractured churches into ever smaller remnants, each certain it has kept the wall. Numbers 6 is a useful corrective: the Nazarite’s separation was for a term, was defined by God down to the grape husk, and ended at the door of the tabernacle with a sacrifice and a return to the congregation. It was a vow within the covenant people, not an exit from them, and it had a boundary drawn by God rather than extended by the man.
roots_summary: The Hebrew nouns differ by context: nezer is the Nazarite’s consecration, niddah the ceremonial uncleanness, and me niddah the water of separation. The unifying root idea is being set apart or put away.
roots_lines: Hebrew nezer (H5145) — consecration, separation, a crown; the Nazarite’s vow and the diadem on the high priest’s mitre (Numbers 6:4, 8, 13).
Hebrew nazir (H5139) — one separated, a Nazarite; the noun for the man under the vow.
Hebrew niddah (H5079) — separation, impurity; the ceremonial state of Leviticus 12:5 and 15:20.
Hebrew me niddah — water of separation, the ash-water of the red heifer (Numbers 19:21), which cleansed the defiled and defiled the clean.
Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, separate; the verb of Genesis 1 and of Ezekiel’s wall between sanctuary and profane.
usage: All the days of his separation he is holy unto the LORD (Numbers 6:8) — the vow makes the whole period, and the man, a set-apart thing.
The water of separation (Numbers 19:21) — a purifying water that defiled the man who handled it; a type of the cleansing that costs the cleanser.
To make a separation between the sanctuary and the profane place (Ezekiel 42:20) — the distinction built into the architecture.

etymology: From fruit plus -ful. Webster 1828: producing fruit in abundance; prolific; fertile. In the Authorized Version the word belongs first to a blessing and a command given at creation and repeated after the flood, and then to the patriarchal promises and their fulfilment.
biblical_def: Fruitful is the first word of blessing God speaks over living creatures, and it is a command as well as a gift. And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas (Genesis 1:22), and the same blessing is given to man. After the flood it is renewed word for word: God blessed Noah and his sons, and said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth (Genesis 9:1), and pressed again two verses later, be ye fruitful, and multiply; bring forth abundantly in the earth (Genesis 9:7). It then becomes covenant promise: I will make thee exceeding fruitful, and I will make nations of thee, and kings shall come out of thee (Genesis 17:6), passed on to Jacob — I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee (Genesis 35:11). Joseph, who lost everything, names his son for it: God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction (Genesis 41:52), and his father blesses him as a fruitful bough, even a fruitful bough by a well (Genesis 49:22). Fruitfulness in Scripture is therefore never a mere biological fact. It is a blessing spoken, a command given, and a covenant kept.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FRUITFUL as producing fruit in abundance; prolific; fertile; and figuratively, productive of any good or effect. Scripture uses both, and joins them: a fruitful womb and a fruitful life are alike God’s blessing.
webster_full: FRUITFUL, a. — Producing fruit in abundance; as a fruitful tree or soil.
Prolific; bearing children; not barren.
Plenteous; abounding in any thing; productive of any good.

Webster’s second sense — not barren — is what Scripture treats as a blessing and its absence as a grief to be prayed over, from Sarah and Hannah to Elisabeth. The Bible never treats children as an inconvenience to be managed.
scriptures: Genesis 1:22
And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let fowl multiply in the earth.
Genesis 9:1
And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth.
Genesis 17:6
And I will make thee exceeding fruitful, and I will make nations of thee, and kings shall come out of thee.
Genesis 35:11
And God said unto him, I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee, and kings shall come out of thy loins;
Genesis 41:52
And the name of the second called he Ephraim: For God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction. Ephraim: that is, Fruitful
corruption_summary: The blessing is corrupted by an age that treats children as a cost to be minimized and human fruitfulness as a threat to the planet — and, on the other side, by a piety that makes family size a test of faithfulness Scripture never made it.
corruption_paragraphs: God speaks be fruitful and multiply as a blessing before He speaks it as a command, and the two are not in competition. That framing is exactly what the contemporary assumption reverses: children are counted first as expense, career interruption, and environmental burden, and only afterward, if at all, as gift. Scripture’s valuation is the opposite and is stated without hedging — Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward (Psalm 127:3). A church that has absorbed the surrounding calculus will find itself unable to say that plainly, and will quietly stop saying it at all. The renewal of the blessing to Noah after the flood is significant on this point: a world newly emptied by judgment is told to fill again.

The corresponding error is to turn a blessing into a measuring stick. Scripture nowhere makes the number of a couple’s children the index of their faith, and it records godly households of every size, along with barrenness borne by Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and Elisabeth without any suggestion that their faith was deficient. Joseph’s naming of Ephraim points to the wider sense the New Testament develops: God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction. Fruitfulness in Christ is bearing much fruit by abiding in the vine (John 15:5), and it is required of every believer, married or single, with children or without.
roots_summary: The Hebrew verb is parah, to bear fruit or be fruitful, from which Ephraim takes his name; it is paired throughout Genesis with rabah, to multiply or become many.
roots_lines: Hebrew parah (H6509) — to bear fruit, be fruitful; the creation blessing (Genesis 1:22), the Noahic renewal (Genesis 9:1), the patriarchal promise (Genesis 17:6; 35:11).
Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to become many, multiply; the constant partner of parah in the formula.
Hebrew Ephraim (H669) — from the same root parah; Joseph names the son for God’s having made him fruitful in affliction (Genesis 41:52).
Hebrew peri (H6529) — fruit; the fruit of the womb (Psalm 127:3) and the fruit of the ground use the same noun.
Greek karpophoreo (G2592) — to bear fruit; the New Testament extension to holiness and good works (Colossians 1:10).
usage: Be fruitful, and multiply (Genesis 1:22) — spoken as blessing before it is heard as command.
I will make thee exceeding fruitful (Genesis 17:6) — the promise to Abraham, kept in a nation and finally in a Seed.
God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction (Genesis 41:52) — fruitfulness given where it was least expected.

etymology: From Latin multiplicare, to make many-fold. Webster 1828: increased in number; made more numerous. In the Authorized Version it records God keeping His promise to Abraham under conditions designed to prevent it, and later records the same increase in the church under persecution.
biblical_def: Multiplied is the narrative proof that God keeps promises. In Egypt, Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the country of Goshen; and they had possessions therein, and grew, and multiplied exceedingly (Genesis 47:27), and Exodus opens with the summary: the children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and waxed exceeding mighty; and the land was filled with them (Exodus 1:7). Pharaoh sets out to stop it, and the text records the result in one of the great sentences of Scripture: But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew (Exodus 1:12). God deals well with the midwives who feared Him, and the people multiplied, and waxed very mighty (Exodus 1:20). Moses can say at the end, The LORD your God hath multiplied you, and, behold, ye are this day as the stars of heaven for multitude (Deuteronomy 1:10) — the promise of Genesis 15 counted out. The word is also a warning: Deuteronomy 8:13 sets prosperity in the same verb — when thy herds and thy flocks multiply, and thy silver and thy gold is multiplied — and warns what the heart does next. And Luke uses it of the church: the word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem greatly (Acts 6:7).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MULTIPLY as to increase in number; to make more by natural generation or production; and MULTIPLIED as increased in number. Scripture uses it of God’s covenant increase and of the accumulation that tempts.
webster_full: MULTIPLY, v.t. [L. multiplico; multus, many, and plico, to fold.] — To increase in number; to make more by natural generation or production, or by addition.
MULTIPLIED, pp. — Increased in number.

The Latin picture is folding many times over. In Genesis the folding is God’s work and Pharaoh cannot unfold it; in Deuteronomy 8 it is a man’s herds and gold, and the danger is that he will forget who folded them.
scriptures: Genesis 47:27
And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the country of Goshen; and they had possessions therein, and grew, and multiplied exceedingly.
Exodus 1:7
And the children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and waxed exceeding mighty; and the land was filled with them.
Exodus 1:12
But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew. And they were grieved because of the children of Israel.
Deuteronomy 8:13
And when thy herds and thy flocks multiply, and thy silver and thy gold is multiplied, and all that thou hast is multiplied;
Acts 6:7
And the word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem greatly; and a great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What has been lost is the doctrine Exodus 1:12 teaches about opposition — that God’s purposes advance through affliction rather than in spite of it — and the warning of Deuteronomy 8 about what increase does to a heart.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is plain. The lesson that goes missing is Exodus 1:12: the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew. Pharaoh’s policy was rational, sustained, and state-backed, and it produced the opposite of its intention. Scripture repeats the pattern — Joseph sold into Egypt, the scattering of the Jerusalem church that spread the gospel, Paul’s bonds which fell out to the furtherance of the gospel. The doctrine is providence: God is not merely able to repair what opposition damages but uses the opposition itself as the means. A church under pressure that concludes God’s work has stalled has forgotten the first chapter of Exodus.

The principle to recover on the other side is Deuteronomy 8. The same verb that describes God’s blessing describes the herds, flocks, silver, and gold that multiply — and the chapter goes on: then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God. Increase is more dangerous to faith than affliction, which is why Moses spends the chapter warning a people about to enter a good land rather than a people in a wilderness. Acts 6:7 shows the increase God delights in: the word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied. The order in that sentence is the safeguard — the word first, and the numbers as its fruit.
roots_summary: The Hebrew is rabah, to become many, the standing partner of parah in the creation and covenant formula; the Greek in Acts is plethuno, to make full or increase.
roots_lines: Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to be or become many, to multiply; the covenant verb of Genesis 47:27, Exodus 1:7, 12, 20, and Deuteronomy 1:10.
Hebrew parah (H6509) — to be fruitful; the constant companion of rabah in the formula be fruitful and multiply.
Hebrew sharats (H8317) — to swarm, teem; the vivid verb rendered increased abundantly in Exodus 1:7.
Greek plethuno (G4129) — to increase, to multiply; the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem greatly (Acts 6:7).
Greek auxano (G837) — to grow, increase; the word of God increased in the same verse, and the ordinary word for the growth of the church.
usage: The more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew (Exodus 1:12) — opposition made the means of the promise.
Thy silver and thy gold is multiplied (Deuteronomy 8:13) — the same verb, now a warning about the heart.
The word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied (Acts 6:7) — the order of the two clauses is the safeguard.

etymology: From off plus spring, that which springs from. Webster 1828: a child or children; a descendant or descendants, however remote from the stock; and, figuratively, production of any kind. The Authorized Version uses it of a man’s posterity, of the human race as God’s creation, and once of Christ Himself.
biblical_def: Offspring in the Old Testament is a man’s posterity, and it is normally paired with seed. Eliphaz promises Job, thy seed shall be great, and thine offspring as the grass of the earth (Job 5:25), and Job later observes the wicked whose seed is established in their sight with them, and their offspring before their eyes (Job 21:8). Isaiah makes it the object of covenant promise: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring (Isaiah 44:3), and their seed shall be known among the Gentiles, and their offspring among the people: all that see them shall acknowledge them, that they are the seed which the LORD hath blessed (Isaiah 61:9). In the New Testament Paul stands on Mars’ hill and quotes a Greek poet back at the Athenians: as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring (Acts 17:28), and draws the conclusion at once: Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device (Acts 17:29). The last use is the Lord’s own: I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star (Revelation 22:16) — David’s descendant and David’s origin at once.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OFFSPRING as a child or children; a descendant or descendants, however remote from the stock; and, figuratively, production of any kind. The word is native English for what Scripture usually calls seed.
webster_full: OFFSPRING, n. — A child or children; a descendant or descendants, however remote from the stock.
Production of any kind; as, the offspring of the brain.
The word is a compound of off and spring — that which springs off from a stock — and it carries the same botanical picture as the biblical seed, branch, and root.
scriptures: Job 5:25
Thou shalt know also that thy seed shall be great, and thine offspring as the grass of the earth.
Isaiah 44:3
For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring:
Isaiah 61:9
And their seed shall be known among the Gentiles, and their offspring among the people: all that see them shall acknowledge them, that they are the seed which the LORD hath blessed.
Acts 17:29
Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device.
Revelation 22:16
I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star.
corruption_summary: Acts 17:28 is corrupted when Paul’s we are also his offspring is made a doctrine of universal spiritual sonship — every person a child of God in the saving sense — which is precisely the opposite of the argument Paul builds on it.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul quotes the poet Aratus to establish creaturely dependence, not saving sonship, and the very next sentence shows what he is doing with it: since we are God’s offspring, we must not imagine the Godhead is like gold or silver graven by art. The argument is against idolatry, and it ends with a command: God… now commandeth all men every where to repent: because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness (Acts 17:30-31). The universal fatherhood of God in the liberal sense — all men saved sons, needing only to realize it — takes Paul’s premise and deletes his conclusion. John draws the distinction the New Testament actually teaches: as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name (John 1:12). All men are God’s creatures and image-bearers; not all are His sons by adoption.

The positive doctrine in the word is worth keeping, because it grounds human dignity where Scripture grounds it. Every human being is God’s offspring by creation, which is why murder is an assault on God’s image (Genesis 9:6) and why Athens’ idols were an insult to the Athenians as well as to God. And Revelation 22:16 keeps the deepest paradox in the word: Christ is at once the root and the offspring of David — the source from which David sprang and the descendant who sprang from him. That is the mystery our Lord pressed on the Pharisees from Psalm 110, and it is why the genealogies and the eternal generation of the Son must be held together.
roots_summary: The Hebrew is usually tse'etsa', that which comes forth, paired with zera', seed; the Greek is genos, kind or race, in Acts 17 and the botanical genos again in Revelation 22:16.
roots_lines: Hebrew tse'etsa' (H6631) — that which issues, offspring, produce; Job 5:25, Isaiah 44:3, Isaiah 61:9.
Hebrew zera' (H2233) — seed; the constant partner of tse'etsa', and the word of the protevangelium in Genesis 3:15.
Greek genos (G1085) — kind, race, stock, offspring; we are also his offspring (Acts 17:28-29) and the offspring of David (Revelation 22:16).
Greek rhiza (G4491) — root; the paired title in Revelation 22:16 and the root of Jesse of Isaiah 11:10.
The pairing of root and offspring in one title asserts both the eternal deity of the Son and His true descent from David according to the flesh.
usage: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring (Isaiah 44:3) — covenant blessing reaching the generations.
Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God (Acts 17:29) — creaturely dependence used as an argument against idols, not for universal sonship.
I am the root and the offspring of David (Revelation 22:16) — David’s source and David’s descendant in one Person.

etymology: From Latin natura, from nasci, to be born. Webster 1828: the essential qualities of a thing; the established course of things; also, natural affection, and the state of man as born, unregenerate. The New Testament uses the word in three distinct ways, and confusing them causes real doctrinal damage.
biblical_def: The New Testament’s nature has three senses. First, what a thing essentially is: the Gentiles are Jews by nature or not (Galatians 2:15); idols are by nature no gods (Galatians 4:8); Christ took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham (Hebrews 2:16). Second, the created order as a moral witness: the Gentiles do by nature the things contained in the law and are thereby a law unto themselves (Romans 2:14), and Paul appeals to it in the assembly — Doth not even nature itself teach you? (1 Corinthians 11:14). Third, and most weightily, the state of man as born: we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh… and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others (Ephesians 2:3). That is original sin stated in a phrase — not what men become by bad choices but what they are by birth. Paul also uses the word to condemn what the age most defends: God gave them up unto vile affections: for even their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature (Romans 1:26). Nature here is not statistics or instinct but the Creator’s design read off the creature.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives NATURE as the essential qualities or attributes of a thing; the established course of things; the constitution and state of man as born, unregenerate; and natural affection. All four senses appear in the New Testament.
webster_full: NATURE, n. [L. natura, from nascor, to be born.] — In a general sense, whatever is made or produced; the whole system of created things.
The essential qualities or attributes of a thing which constitute it what it is; as, the nature of the soul; the nature of God.
The established or regular course of things; as, when we say an event is not according to nature.
The constitution and state of man as born; the state of unregeneracy — as, we are by nature children of wrath.
Natural affection or reverence; as, a man void of natural affection.
Webster’s fourth sense quotes Ephesians 2:3 almost verbatim and shows how thoroughly the doctrine had shaped the language.
scriptures: Romans 1:26
For this cause God gave them up unto vile affections: for even their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature:
Romans 2:14
For when the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law, these, having not the law, are a law unto themselves:
Galatians 4:8
Howbeit then, when ye knew not God, ye did service unto them which by nature are no gods.
Ephesians 2:3
Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others.
Hebrews 2:16
For verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham.
corruption_summary: The word is corrupted when natural is redefined from as God designed it to as I find myself — a move that makes Romans 1:26 unreadable and turns every inclination into a warrant.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 1:26 measures conduct against nature, meaning the creational design legible in the bodies God made — the same design Genesis 1:27 states as male and female and Matthew 19:4 has our Lord citing. The affirming readings of Scripture associated with Vines and Brownson must relocate the standard: natural becomes what is natural to a person, that is, what he or she experiences as native desire. On that definition Paul’s argument evaporates, since no one acts against his own inclinations by definition. But Paul is not describing what feels foreign to the agent; he is describing what departs from the use for which the Creator formed the body, which is why he says the natural use and not their natural use. The dictionary holds the historic position: sex is the creational, embodied category, marriage is one man and one woman, and pastoral care for image-bearers caught in sin is a wholly different thing from doctrinal approval of the sin.

Ephesians 2:3 guards against the self-righteousness that can attach to the paragraph above. We all had our conversation in times past… and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others. The apostle includes himself and his readers, and the phrase by nature makes the condition prior to any particular sin. Original sin is not a doctrine about other people’s vices; it is the account of what every human being is from birth apart from grace, and it is the reason regeneration and not reformation is required. A church that names sin accurately and forgets Ephesians 2:3 will name it cruelly, and a church that remembers Ephesians 2:3 and will not name sin has kept the humility and lost the gospel.
roots_summary: The Greek phusis means what a thing is by birth or growth, from phuo, to bring forth; it covers essence, the created order, and the inherited condition of fallen man.
roots_lines: Greek phusis (G5449) — nature, native constitution; Romans 1:26, Romans 2:14, Galatians 4:8, Ephesians 2:3.
Greek phusikos (G5446) — natural, according to nature; the adjective in Romans 1:26-27, the natural use.
Greek para phusin — against nature; the phrase in Romans 1:26, measured against the created design and not against personal inclination.
Greek epilambanomai in Hebrews 2:16 — to take hold of; the KJV supplies the nature of to render he taketh hold of the seed of Abraham.
Greek theias phuseos — the divine nature of 2 Peter 1:4, where partaking is moral likeness, not participation in the divine essence.
usage: Were by nature the children of wrath, even as others (Ephesians 2:3) — original sin in a phrase; the condition precedes the conduct.
Which by nature are no gods (Galatians 4:8) — nature as what a thing essentially is.
He took on him the seed of Abraham (Hebrews 2:16) — the incarnation assumed our nature and not the angels’.

etymology: From willing, from will. Webster 1828: with free will; without reluctance; cheerfully. The Authorized Version attaches it to the two things God most cares to have freely: the offerings that built the tabernacle and the temple, and the men who volunteered for battle.
biblical_def: God asks for the tabernacle materials on one condition: of every man that giveth it willingly with his heart ye shall take my offering (Exodus 25:2). The condition is not the amount. Deborah’s song praises the same thing twice — Praise ye the LORD for the avenging of Israel, when the people willingly offered themselves (Judges 5:2), and My heart is toward the governors of Israel, that offered themselves willingly among the people (Judges 5:9). Amasiah is remembered for it: who willingly offered himself unto the LORD with two hundred thousand mighty men (2 Chronicles 17:16). David’s temple collection is the fullest case: the chiefs offered willingly (1 Chronicles 29:6), the people rejoiced, for that they offered willingly, because with perfect heart they offered willingly to the LORD (1 Chronicles 29:9), and David’s prayer removes any ground of boasting: who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee (1 Chronicles 29:14). The New Testament carries it into the eldership: a pastor is to take the oversight not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind (1 Peter 5:2). Its one negative use is a mercy: the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly (Romans 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WILLINGLY as with free will; without reluctance; cheerfully; and, by extension, of choice rather than of compulsion. Scripture attaches it to giving, to volunteering, and to the pastoral office.
webster_full: WILLINGLY, adv. — With free will; without reluctance; cheerfully.
By one’s own choice; spontaneously; as, he came willingly.
WILLING, a. — Free to do or grant; having the mind inclined; disposed; not averse.
Webster’s without reluctance is the biblical requirement in giving, and 1 Chronicles 29:14 keeps it from becoming a boast: the willingness itself is a gift, and what is given was God’s already.
scriptures: Judges 5:2
Praise ye the LORD for the avenging of Israel, when the people willingly offered themselves.
Judges 5:9
My heart is toward the governors of Israel, that offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless ye the LORD.
1 Chronicles 29:9
Then the people rejoiced, for that they offered willingly, because with perfect heart they offered willingly to the LORD: and David the king also rejoiced with great joy.
Romans 8:20
For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope,
1 Peter 5:2
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
corruption_summary: Willing giving is corrupted from both ends: by manipulation that manufactures the appearance of willingness, and by the notion that willingness is a substitute for the act — a heart that intends to give and never does.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 25:2 and 1 Chronicles 29 record giving that was neither taxed nor pressured, and the joy in the second passage is inseparable from the freedom in it: the people rejoiced, for that they offered willingly. Fund-raising that works by pressure, shame, guaranteed returns, or public comparison produces the amount and destroys the thing God asked for. Paul states the rule for the church without softening it: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). Prosperity appeals are the sharpest form of the corruption, since they replace willingness with expected return — and 1 Peter 5:2 forbids the same motive in a pastor, not for filthy lucre.

The opposite corruption is a willingness that never becomes an act. Judges 5 praises the people who offered themselves, and the same song curses Meroz for staying home and reproaches Reuben for great searchings of heart while others fought. A disposition that remains a disposition is not what the word describes. And David’s prayer forecloses pride in either direction: who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee. The willingness is itself God’s gift — it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13) — which leaves the cheerful giver nothing to boast of and every reason to give.
roots_summary: The Hebrew root nadab means to impel or volunteer, and gives the noun for a freewill offering; the Greek hekousios in 1 Peter 5:2 means voluntarily, set against constraint.
roots_lines: Hebrew nadab (H5068) — to incite, impel, volunteer; the people willingly offered themselves (Judges 5:2, 9) and offered willingly (1 Chronicles 29:6, 9).
Hebrew nedabah (H5071) — a freewill offering; the noun from the same root, a whole class of sacrifice defined by its voluntariness.
Hebrew nadib (H5081) — noble, willing-hearted; the adjective in whosoever is of a willing heart (Exodus 35:5).
Greek hekousios (G1596) — voluntarily, willingly; not by constraint, but willingly (1 Peter 5:2).
Greek hekon (G1635) — willing, of one’s own accord; the negative in Romans 8:20, not willingly, of the creation subjected to vanity.
usage: Of every man that giveth it willingly with his heart (Exodus 25:2) — the condition on the tabernacle offering is the manner, not the amount.
With perfect heart they offered willingly to the LORD (1 Chronicles 29:9) — free giving and public rejoicing together.
Not by constraint, but willingly (1 Peter 5:2) — the same requirement laid on the man who takes the oversight.

etymology: A compound coined for the English Bible: a block over which one stumbles. Webster 1828: any cause of stumbling; that which causes to err or sin. It renders the Hebrew mikshol and the Greek skandalon, the trigger-stick of a trap, and the KJV’s compound has passed into ordinary English from the Bible.
biblical_def: The law forbids the literal thing and means the figurative: Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind, but shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD (Leviticus 19:14) — a cruelty the victim cannot see coming, and the prohibition is sealed with the fear of God. Ezekiel finds men who have made their own: these men have set up their idols in their heart, and put the stumblingblock of their iniquity before their face (Ezekiel 14:3). Isaiah’s command to the highway-builders is to clear it: take up the stumblingblock out of the way of my people (Isaiah 57:14). The New Testament makes it a governing rule of Christian liberty. Judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way (Romans 14:13); take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak (1 Corinthians 8:9). And there is one stumblingblock that must never be removed: we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness (1 Corinthians 1:23). The cross itself offends, and that offence is not a fault in the message to be engineered away.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines STUMBLINGBLOCK as any cause of stumbling; that which causes to err or to sin; and notes it as a scriptural term. The compound entered English from the English Bible.
webster_full: STUMBLINGBLOCK, n. — Any cause of stumbling; that which causes to stumble, err, or sin.
STUMBLINGSTONE, n. — The same; as in Romans 9:32, they stumbled at that stumblingstone.
The word is one of Tyndale’s compounds, kept by the Authorized Version and passed from there into common English usage — one of many phrases the English Bible gave the language.
scriptures: Leviticus 19:14
Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind, but shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD.
Isaiah 57:14
And shall say, Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way, take up the stumblingblock out of the way of my people.
Ezekiel 14:3
Son of man, these men have set up their idols in their heart, and put the stumblingblock of their iniquity before their face: should I be enquired of at all by them?
Romans 14:13
Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way.
1 Corinthians 1:23
But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;
corruption_summary: Romans 14:13 is corrupted when the weak brother’s conscience becomes a veto that any offended party may claim, and 1 Corinthians 1:23 when the offence of the cross is treated as a stumblingblock to be cleared away rather than the one that must remain.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s rule in Romans 14 concerns a genuinely weak brother — a believer whose conscience is not yet instructed and who would be led to act against it. It is not a general licence for anyone who takes offence to govern the church’s practice. Paul himself refused to yield an inch when the issue was the gospel: we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour (Galatians 2:5), and he rebuked Peter publicly over the same matter. The distinction is between wounding a weak conscience, which love forbids, and offending a strong opinion, which love sometimes requires. A church that cannot tell the two apart will either trample the weak or be ruled by the loudest.

The second corruption is the more serious. Christ crucified is called unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness, and Paul reports this as a description of his preaching rather than a problem with it. Every generation is tempted to remove that particular block — by making the atonement a moral example, by preaching a Christ who came chiefly to affirm, by leaving the wrath of God and the substitution out of the message so that the offence is gone. What is left may fill a room, but it is not the power of God unto salvation. The apostolic pattern is to remove every stumblingblock a man puts in his brother’s way, and to leave standing the one God Himself has laid — the stone of stumbling on which men either fall or are built.
roots_summary: The Hebrew mikshol is an obstacle that trips; the Greek skandalon was the trigger-stick of a trap, and gives English scandal. Both name something that causes a fall, not merely something that gives offence.
roots_lines: Hebrew mikshol (H4383) — a stumbling, an obstacle; Leviticus 19:14, Isaiah 57:14, Ezekiel 14:3.
Hebrew kashal (H3782) — to stumble, totter, fall; the verb behind the noun.
Greek skandalon (G4625) — the trigger-stick of a trap, hence a snare or cause of stumbling; Romans 14:13, 1 Corinthians 1:23.
Greek proskomma (G4348) — an occasion of stumbling; paired with skandalon in Romans 14:13 as an occasion to fall.
Greek lithos proskommatos — a stone of stumbling; Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8, quoting Isaiah 8:14 of Christ.
usage: Nor put a stumblingblock before the blind, but shalt fear thy God (Leviticus 19:14) — cruelty the victim cannot foresee, forbidden on pain of God’s notice.
No man put a stumblingblock… in his brother's way (Romans 14:13) — the rule governing the use of Christian liberty.
Unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness (1 Corinthians 1:23) — the one offence the church may not remove.
